note: ep10 'The Nguyens: Social Security at 62 or 70?' (2026-11-13). Uncle Tu turns 62 (born 1964, full retirement age 67). His check: $2,000 a month at 67 in today's money, so $1,400 at 62 (70%) and $2,480 at 70 (124%), SSA claiming table for births 1960+. All dollars are today's money: checks rise with prices (COLA). Uncle Tu is single and stops working at 62. Part 1: take it at 62 vs wait to 70, plain checks: break-even and SSA's 2023 period life table. Part 2: Minh's way, take it at 62 and invest every check in stocks; from 70 the pile tops him up to $2,480 until it runs out. Two real replays (turned 62 in 1990-01 and 2000-01) and every start month 1871-01..1988-06 followed to 100. Lines in race/replay scenes carry `month` = months since his 62nd birthday. Speakers: N narrator, M Minh, L Lan, T Uncle Tu. Bin is silent: his card is on screen. Every spoken number is checked by tools/validate-ep10-story.mjs. `*word*` = emphasis. The family are illustrations.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Today Uncle Tu turns *sixty-two*. That means he can start Social Security. And the letter just came.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Take it now, at sixty-two: *fourteen hundred dollars* a month. Wait until sixty-seven: two thousand. Wait until seventy: *twenty-four hundred eighty*. Every year he waits, the check gets bigger. And every year, it rises with prices. Next year's raise was just announced: three point six percent.

lines.speaker: T
lines.text: I take it now. A bird in the hand.

lines.speaker: L
lines.text: But at seventy, it's almost *eighty percent* more. For the rest of your life.

lines.speaker: T
lines.text: Who knows if I'm still here at eighty?

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Or take it now, and *invest* it. Best of both.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Three ideas. Let's check them one at a time, in today's money. Uncle Tu is single, and he stops working at sixty-two, so he lives on his savings until the check starts. First question: take it now, or wait until seventy?

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Here's the race. On the left, Uncle Tu's way: a check every month from sixty-two. On the right, Lan's way: nothing until seventy.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: By seventy, Uncle Tu's way has collected *a hundred thirty-four thousand dollars*. Lan's way: zero.

lines.speaker: T
lines.text: See? I'm way ahead.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: But now Lan's check is bigger, by *one thousand eighty dollars*, every month. A little past *eighty*, the two piles are even.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: At ninety, Lan's way is ahead by about *a hundred twenty-five thousand*.

lines.speaker: L
lines.text: So waiting wins if you live past eighty.

lines.speaker: T
lines.text: *If.* That's the bet.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: So how long do people actually live? Social Security keeps the table. Here are a hundred men in the US who just turned sixty-two, like Uncle Tu.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: By eighty, about *six in ten* are still here. On average, a man lives to about *eighty-two*. For women, it's about seven in ten, and about eighty-five.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And averaged over how long people really live, waiting until seventy paid men about *forty thousand dollars* more. Women, about seventy thousand more.

lines.speaker: T
lines.text: But if I die at seventy, I got nothing!

lines.speaker: L
lines.text: If you die early, you won't be around to miss it. What scares me is ninety-five, on the small check.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And that's the twist. Waiting isn't a bet that you'll live long. It's *insurance*, in case you do. At ninety-five, Lan's way is ahead by about a hundred ninety thousand.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Okay. But what about my idea? Take it at sixty-two, and invest every check.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Here's Minh's way. From sixty-two to seventy, every check goes into stocks. From seventy on, the pile tops him up to the big check, twenty-four eighty a month, the same as Lan's way. As long as the pile lasts, Minh's way keeps up, and whatever is left is extra. If the pile runs out, he's back to fourteen hundred, for life.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Let's replay real history. Say Uncle Tu turned sixty-two in January nineteen ninety.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The nineties boom. By seventy, his pile is about *two hundred seventy thousand*. He only put in a hundred thirty-four.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Told you!

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: June twenty twenty-six. He's ninety-eight. He took his top-up every single month, and the pile still has about *two hundred thirty-six thousand*. Minh's way wins, big.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Now say he turned sixty-two ten years later. January two thousand.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The dot-com crash. By fall twenty oh two, he's put in forty-six thousand, and the pile is worth about *thirty-three thousand*.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: It comes back. At seventy, about a hundred forty-nine thousand. Then, two thousand eight.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: March two thousand nine. About *seventy-two thousand* left, and he still takes his top-up every month.

lines.speaker: T
lines.text: December twenty twenty-three. I'm almost eighty-six. *The pile is empty.*

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: From here on, Minh's way pays fourteen hundred a month. Lan's way pays twenty-four eighty, for as long as he lives.

lines.speaker: L
lines.text: So in one history, Minh's way wins big. In the other, the money runs out at eighty-six.

lines.speaker: T
lines.text: Two years prove nothing. Check them all.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: So we did. Every month since eighteen seventy-one when someone could turn sixty-two, invest the checks, and be followed to a hundred: *fourteen hundred and ten* starts. Each square is one start. Its colour says when the pile ran out.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In a little under *half*, the money lasted to a hundred. There, Minh's way won. But in about *one in three*, it ran out before ninety. About one in five, before eighty-five. The worst start: January nineteen sixty-six. High inflation and bad markets emptied the pile at *seventy-eight*.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: So investing the early checks is a bet on the stock market. Waiting buys a check that rises with prices and lasts as long as you do.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And Bin, who hasn't said a word this whole time, hands Uncle Tu his birthday card.

lines.speaker: T
lines.text: A hundred? Then I'd better wait.

lines.speaker: L
lines.text: Happy birthday, Uncle Tu.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: So what does this mean for you? *Lesson one.* The break-even is about eighty. Most people who reach sixty-two live past it: about six in ten men, and seven in ten women.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: *Lesson two.* Waiting is insurance against a long life. The bigger check rises with prices, and it lasts as long as you do.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: *Lesson three.* Taking it early and investing it can work. The money lasted to a hundred in a little under half of history. But about one time in three, it ran out before ninety, right when the big check matters most. And if your health is poor, or you need the money now, taking it early can be the right call.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Here's what we assumed. Uncle Tu's check is two thousand dollars a month at sixty-seven, in today's money, the rule for anyone born in nineteen sixty or later. Every check rises with prices. He is single, stops working at sixty-two, and pays no taxes. Social Security pays in full, as promised. Lifespans come from Social Security's twenty twenty-three life table; people turning sixty-two today will likely live a bit longer. Stocks are the S and P with dividends, no fees. For married couples, waiting also raises the check a widow or widower keeps. The family are illustrations. The history is real. This is history, not advice.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Would you take it at sixty-two, or wait until seventy? Tell me in the comments.
